newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania's Berisha predicts calm, rivals plan rally.
newsitem.headline: Albania's Berisha predicts calm, rivals plan rally.

text.p: Albanian President Sali Berisha predicted on Friday that unrest over failed pyramid investment schemes would abate once distraught depositors got some money back, but the newly united opposition planned fresh protests.

Enraged Albanians, many ruined after placing their life savings in the funds, have staged violent protests throughout the Balkan country, denouncing Berisha over his government's handling of the collapsed schemes.

The president, in an interview with Reuters and the British Broadcasting Corporation, repeated pledges that the poorest depositors would be reimbursed in cash. Others would get government certificates or shares, an offer already angrily rejected by many impoverished Albanians.
"We have promised the investors all the frozen money which is in our banks," Berisha said. "There is two-thirds of the money there so they will get the majority of their money back."

Economists believe more than $1.0 billion is tied up in the pyramid saving schemes which began to crumble at the end of last year. Virtually every family in the country of 3.4 million, Europe's poorest state, has invested some money.

"We have never promised full compensation. This could not happen," the rightist Berisha said. "We are definitely decided not to provoke inflation." Inflation hit 17.4 percent in December after starting last year around six percent.

Albania's opposition, undeterred by mass arrests after last week's protests, pledged to go ahead with a rally on Sunday at a soccer stadium in the Adriatic port of Durres, 40 km (25 miles) west of Tirana.

"We are going to hold a protest against the way the government has handled the closure of pyramid scheme companies and ask for the return of all money," said a spokesman in Durres for the Socialist Party, Berisha's main rivals.

Berisha's Democratic Party ousted ex-communists in 1992 elections. It has a virtual stranglehold on parliament after winning nearly 90 percent of the vote in last May's subsequent election criticised as unfair by international observers.

The opposition on Thursday founded the Forum for Democracy, bringing together for the first time socialists, liberals, former political prisoners and other disparate groups with the sole aim of forcing Berisha's government from power.

Berisha accused his main political rivals, the Socialists, of funding their general election campaign last May on money from pyramid schemes -- the same charge the Socialists level at the president's Democratic Party.
Albania's central bank increased short-term money rates on Friday to shore up the country's crumbling lek currency.
The lek has fallen 30 percent against the dollar since the New Year and traders on Tirana's dusty streets have become increasingly reluctant to part with the U.S. currency.
"Since the collapse of the pyramids no one wants the lek, they just want dollars," said Muli, one of about 500 such dealers, clutching a wad of colourful leks in his fist.
Judicial authorities have said 149 people have been arrested and charged with violence, theft and damaging public property in three weeks of unrest, mostly in southern regions.
Government buildings and offices of Berisha's Democratic Party were set on fire in rioting last weekend.

A witness in the town of Gjirokaster, on the Greek border, said police were checking hotels to ferret out suspected rioters. "Police checked the identity of guests against long lists of suspects to prevent anyone from fleeing to Greece," he said.
